'''Professor Sir Carlos Silvestre Frenk''' {{post-nominals|country=GBR|size=100%|CBE|FRS}} (born 27 October 1951) is a Mexican-British [[cosmologist]].<ref name="whoswho">{{Who's Who | author=Anon| title=Frenk, Prof. Carlos Silvestre  | id = U16471 | year = 2017 | doi =10.1093/ww/9780199540884.013.U16471 | edition = online [[Oxford University Press]]|location=Oxford}}</ref> whose research has focused on galaxy formation, dark matter and the large-scale structure of the Universe. He contributed to the development of the Cold Dark Matter paradigm and co-developed the [[Navarro–Frenk–White profile]] with [[Julio Navarro (astrophysicist)|Julio Navarro]] and [[Simon White]]. He has been Ogden Professor of Fundamental Physics at [[Durham University]] since 2001 and served as founding Director of the [[Institute for Computational Cosmology]] from 2001 to 2020.<ref name="CV">{{Cite web |title=Carlos Frenk CV |url=http://star-www.dur.ac.uk/~csf/homepage/cv.pdf}}</ref> Frenk is a co-founder of the [[Virgo Consortium]], an international collaboration that carries out large-scale cosmological simulations, including the Millennium Simulation. He has also participated in the [[Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument]] (DESI) collaboration and has been associated with large numerical simulation projects including FLAMINGO and COLIBRE. He was elected a Fellow of the [[Royal Society]] in 2004, appointed Commander of the [[Order of the British Empire]] (CBE) in the 2017 [[Birthday Honours]] for services to cosmology, and knighted as a Knight Bachelor in the 2026 Birthday Honours for services to astrophysics and cosmology.

==Early life and education==
Frenk was born in [[Mexico City]], Mexico.<ref name=gruber>{{cite web |date=2011 |title=Carlos Frenk |url=https://gruber.yale.edu/recipient/carlos-frenk |access-date=19 September 2025 |website=[[Gruber Foundation]]}}</ref> His father was a German-Jewish physician who emigrated before the Second World War, and his mother was a Mexican pianist.<ref name="BBC-Radio4">{{Cite web |title=Professor Carlos Frenk |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b0b5s44q |access-date=28 September 2021 |website=Desert Island Discs |publisher=BBC Radio 4}}</ref> He studied engineering and later theoretical physics at the at the [[National Autonomous University of Mexico]] (UNAM), graduating in 1976 with the [[Gabino Barreda Medal]].<ref name="scwprofile">{{cite web |date=8 May 2008 |title=The universe in a desktop |url=https://www.scientific-computing.com/feature/universe-desktop |access-date=27 April 2023 |website=Scientific Computing World |publisher=Europa Science Ltd}}</ref>. He subsequently moved to the University of Cambridge on a British Council Fellowship, completing [[Part III of the Mathematical Tripos]] and receiving a PhD in 1981 under the supervision of Bernard J. T. Jones focusing on globular clusters.<ref name="mathgene">{{MathGenealogy|id=156129}}</ref>

His younger brother, Julio Frenk, is a physician and academic administrator who has served as Mexico's Minister of Health, President of the University of Miami, and Chancellor of the University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA). 

==Career==
After his doctorate, Frenk held research positions [[University of California, Berkeley]], where he collaborated with [[Marc Davis (astronomer)|Marc Davis]] on galaxy surveys. In 1983, Frenk, Davis, and [[Simon White]] published work showing that neutrinos could not account for dark matter.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=White |first1=Simon |last2=Frenk |first2=Carlos |last3=Davis |first3=Marc |date=November 1983 |title=Clustering in a neutrino-dominated universe |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |volume=274 |pages=L1–L5 |doi=10.1086/184139 |bibcode=1983ApJ...274L...1W}}</ref> He later held posts at the [[University of California, Santa Barbara]] and the [[University of Sussex]].<ref name=gruber />

With Davis, White, and [[George Efstathiou]], Frenk helped develop early simulations supporting the [[cold dark matter]] (CDM) model. A 1985 paper in ''[[The Astrophysical Journal]]'' presented the first large-scale CDM simulations.<ref name="darkmatterhist">{{cite web |author1=Gianfranco Bertone |author2=Dan Hooper |title=A History of Dark Matter |url=https://ned.ipac.caltech.edu/level5/Sept16/Bertone/paper.pdf |publisher=[[Fermilab]] |access-date=28 April 2023 |page=61 |date=24 May 2016}}</ref> 

In 1986, Frenk joined [[Durham University]], becoming professor in 1993. In 1994 he and White co-founded the [[Virgo Consortium]] for cosmological simulations.<ref name=scwprofile />

===Navarro–Frenk–White profile===
In 1996 and 1997, Frenk, White, and [[Julio Navarro (astrophysicist)|Julio Navarro]] described the [[Navarro–Frenk–White profile]], which characterises the distribution of dark matter in halos and is widely used in cosmology.<ref name=darkmatterhist />

===Later work===
In 2001, Frenk became the first Ogden Professor of Fundamental Physics at Durham and founding director of the [[Institute for Computational Cosmology]], a post he held until 2020.<ref name=CV /> He was part of the Virgo Consortium’s [[Millennium Run]] project and continues to work on large-scale simulations of galaxy formation.

==Personal life==
Frenk is married to Lady Dr. Susan Frenk, a lecturer in Spanish and Latin American literature and Principal of [[St Aidan's College, Durham]]. They have two sons.<ref name="the">{{cite web |title=A marriage of minds |url=https://www.timeshighereducation.com/news/a-marriage-of-minds/154488.article |website=[[Times Higher Education (THE)]] |access-date=24 April 2023 |date=4 November 1994}}</ref>    

==Honours==
Frenk was elected a [[Fellow of the Royal Society]] (FRS) in 2004.<ref>{{cite web |title=Carlos Frenk |url=https://royalsociety.org/people/carlos-frenk-11462/ |website=[[Royal Society]] |access-date=27 April 2023}}</ref> He was appointed [[Commander of the Order of the British Empire]] (CBE) in the [[2017 Birthday Honours]] for services to cosmology<ref>{{London Gazette|issue=61962|supp=y|page=B8|date=17 June 2017}}</ref>, and was [[Knight Bachelor|knighted]] in the [[2026 Birthday Honours]] for services to astrophysics and cosmology.<ref>{{Cite web |last=University |first=Durham |title=Knighthood for world-leading cosmologist Professor Carlos Frenk - Durham University |url=https://www.durham.ac.uk/news-events/latest-news/2026/06/knighthood-for-world-leading-cosmologist-professor-carlos-frenk/ |access-date=2026-06-16 |website=www.durham.ac.uk |language=en-gb}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=The King's Birthday Honours List 2026 |url=https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/the-kings-birthday-honours-list-2026 |access-date=2026-06-16 |website=GOV.UK |language=en}}</ref>

He has received the [[Gold Medal of the Royal Astronomical Society]] (2014), the [[Royal Society Wolfson Research Merit Award]] (2006), the Daniel Chalonge Medal (2007), the [[George Darwin Lectureship]] (2010), the [[Fred Hoyle Medal and Prize]] (2010), the [[Gruber Prize in Cosmology]] (2011), the [[Max Born Prize]] (2017), the [[Dirac Medal (IOP)|Dirac Medal and Prize]] (2020), and the [[Rumford Medal]] (2021).<ref name="ras_gold_medal">{{Cite journal |title=RAS Awards 2014 |journal=Astronomy & Geophysics |volume=55 |date=February 2014 |pages=1.37–1.38 |doi=10.1093/astrogeo/atu040|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=Fred Hoyle Medal and Prize recipients |url=https://www.iop.org/about/awards/silver-subject-medals/fred-hoyle-medal-and-prize-recipients |website=[[Institute of Physics]] |access-date=2023-03-21}}</ref><ref name=gruber /><ref>{{Cite web |title=Born medal recipients |url=https://www.iop.org/about/awards/international-bilateral-awards/max-born-medal-and-prize-recipients |access-date=21 March 2023 |website=Institute of Physics}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |title=2020 Paul Dirac Medal and Prize |url=https://www.iop.org/about/awards/gold-medals/paul-dirac-medal-and-prize-recipients |access-date=21 March 2023 |work=Institute of Physics}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.durham.ac.uk/research/current/research-news/carlos-frenk-royal-society-award/|website=Durham University|title=Prestigious Award for Galaxy Evolution Research|date=24 August 2021|access-date=21 March 2023}}</ref>

In 2023 he was named an Honorary Fellow of [[King's College, Cambridge]].<ref>{{cite journal |title=Honorary Fellows |journal=Annual Report 2023 |date=2023 |page=10 |url=https://www.kings.cam.ac.uk/sites/default/files/documents/intranet/kings-annual-report-2023-intranet.pdf |access-date=15 May 2025 |publisher=[[King's College, Cambridge]]}}</ref>

==Public engagement==
Frenk has appeared on television and radio, including ''[[The Sky at Night]]'' and BBC Radio 4’s ''[[Desert Island Discs]]'' in 2018.<ref name="BBC-Radio4" />
